court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: Construing the 1860 act 'for the protection of boarding house keepers,' the court held that a boarding house keeper has the same lien on a boarder's effects brought onto the premises to furnish his room as the common law gives an innkeeper over a guest's goods, even where those goods actually belong to a third party. The judgment for the plaintiff (the boarder's mother) was reversed and a new trial granted.

quotes.text: It was the intention of the legislature, by that act, to give hoarding house keepers the same lien, in respect, to the effects of their hoarders, as the common law gave to innkeepers, as to the goods of their guests.
The defendant has a lien upon the goods in question. They were brought by the boarder upon his premises to furnish his room, and the defendant was the boarding house keeper.

Since the act of April 16, 1860, “ for the protection of boarding house keepers,” the keeper of a boarding house has a lien for hoard, upon goods brought upon the premises by a hoarder, to furnish his room,' although they in fact do not belong to the hoarder, hut to a stranger.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The court held that an emigrant boarding house/inn keeper who instructed a lodger to deposit his baggage with the clerk for safekeeping was not liable when the lodger instead put it under his own bed and it was stolen during his brief absence. A guest who is instructed to place baggage in a particular safe place and neglects to do so cannot recover from the keeper for its loss.

quotes.text: He received every person that came, accommodating them by the day or by the week at a charge of one dollar per day.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The court held that a public house designated a 'hotel,' which provided lodging to guests for uncertain periods under no express agreement and differed from an ordinary hotel only in having an on-premises refectory where guests could separately pay for meals, was an inn, and its proprietor an innkeeper subject to full innkeeper liability as to lodged guests. Compliance with the 1855 statute requiring a safe and posted notice did not relieve the innkeeper of liability for a guest's stolen watch and cash under the facts found by the jury.

quotes.text: A public house, which the proprietor designates as a “ hotel,” and at which guests are provided with lodgings for uncertain periods, and under no express agreement, and which only differs from ordinary hotels in having a refectory on the premises, where guests are at liberty to take their meals, if they wish, and pay for them, then and there: Held, To be an inn, and the proprietor an innkeeper, with all the responsibilities attaching to such character, as respects guests received and accommodated with lodgings.

His house is open to all persons, and he receives them without any express agreement. Travelers go to his premises, and find the ordinary appearances and arrangements of a hotel; they register their names on a book of arrivals, as in hotels generally, and are assigned rooms, which they occupy, with their baggage, as long as they choose to remain.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Where several tenants occupy distinct, separate apartments in a single house and hire them from a landlord who also resides there, the house is the landlord's dwelling-house and the common street door is the 'outer door' of every tenant in it. A sheriff who lawfully enters through that outer door may therefore break open the door of an individual tenant's rented apartment to levy execution on that tenant's goods.

quotes.text: The plaintiff hired from Mrs. Brown the three front rooms on the second floor of No. 306 East 114th street, and placed her goods, consisting of household furniture, in those apartments.

When several persons occupy distinct and several apartments in the same house, and hire from a landlord who also resides in the house, the house is the dwelling-house of the landlord, and the street door is the outer door of all the tenants living in the house, and a sheriff who lawfully enters through such outer door may break open the doors of an apartment occupied by any tenant, in order to levy an execution on the goods of such tenant in the room.
